Kassel
kas'el
n. (capital of Hesse-Kassel; where Landgrave Moritz the Learned brought the landgraviate to the Reformed confession in 1605)
German Kassel, recorded as Chassalla, probably from Latin castellum, a fort, or a Germanic cassel, a settlement by the ford of the Fulda.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kassel was the residence of the landgraves of Hesse and became, under Moritz the Learned, the capital of a Reformed state. Moritz, who ruled from 1592, was a prince of real learning—a musician who composed, a patron of mathematics and astronomy, the founder of a court school for the nobility—and he came by study to the conviction that the Reformed doctrine of the Supper and the Reformed reading of the second commandment were the biblical ones. In 1605 he published the points of improvement for his lands and enforced them: images and altars removed from the churches, the Decalogue taught in the Reformed numbering, the bread broken at the Supper, and subscription required of the clergy and the professors. Those who refused lost their places. The reform was genuine, it was resented, and it was one of the causes which drew Hesse-Kassel into the Thirty Years War on the Protestant side, at a cost which included Moritz's own abdication in 1627. The dictionary enters Kassel because the episode states both halves of the German problem exactly: a prince used his authority to establish a truer doctrine, and in doing so confirmed the principle that a prince's authority is the proper instrument for settling doctrine, which is the error that would later be used against the gospel.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a landgrave as a German count having jurisdiction over a territory; subscription as the act of signing one's name in assent; and reformation as a change from worse to better, an amendment of life or doctrine.

expand to see more

LANDGRAVE, n. [G. land and grave, a count.] In Germany, a count or earl; a nobleman having jurisdiction over a territory.

SUBSCRIPTION, n. The act of subscribing; the signing of one's name, as in token of consent or attestation.

REFORMATION, n. [L. reformatio.] Change from worse to better; amendment of life or manners; in church history, the great change of religion in the sixteenth century.

ALTAR, n. [L. altare.] A mount; an elevation of earth, stone or other matter, on which sacrifices were offered.

ABDICATE, v.t. [L. abdico.] To abandon; particularly, to relinquish an office or sovereignty before the term of service has expired.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Psa 2:10 — "Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth."

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

Hab 2:18 — "What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?"

Modern Corruption

Hessian capital where Moritz the Learned enforced the Reformed points of improvement in 1605, removing images and requiring the clergy to subscribe.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is not the doctrine Moritz established, which the dictionary holds, but the instrument he used. The territorial principle—that a prince settles the religion of his land—makes the magistrate the judge of doctrine, and a magistrate who may command the removal of images may also command their restoration; in Bentheim a generation later one did. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) establishes the civil office and does not hand it the keys of the church.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the second commandment and the regulative principle it implies. “What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it” (Hab 2:18) is the prophet's question, and the answer the churches of Europe had given for centuries was that it profited the devotion of the simple. It did not. The dictionary commends the clearing of the Hessian churches and holds that it ought to have been done by the churches themselves, upon conviction, with the prince protecting the work rather than decreeing it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image; Hebrew sakal (H7919), to act wisely, to be prudent.

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image”, Exodus 20:4.

Hebrew temunah (H8544) — a likeness, a form; “or any likeness of any thing”, Exodus 20:4.

Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to be prudent, to act wisely; “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings”, Psalm 2:10.

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, delegated power; “there is no power but of God”, Romans 13:1.

Hebrew massekah (H4541) — a molten image; “the molten image, and a teacher of lies”, Habakkuk 2:18.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the images and altars taken out of the Hessian churches in 1605."

"“Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10) — a learned prince who came to the doctrine by study."

"“Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) — the office established, and the keys withheld."
